name: Holiday lights
summary: Start a holiday light installation business: your first 25 neighbors and partners, a price menu by home size and by the foot from real ranges, a roofline plan with feet of lights, clips, cords and circuits, and the right offer for each month of the year.
door_step3: I hang them, fix any bulb that goes out and take them down in January
door_rule: Door hangers go on the door, never in or on a mailbox: putting unstamped flyers in a mailbox is a federal offense (18 U.S. Code 1725). Check your city rules on door to door flyers.

promises.first_25: 15 people you know and 10 local HOAs, agents, shops, churches and restaurants, each with a message, plus door hangers with the offer that fits the month.
promises.offer: Your price menu by home size and by the foot, the first-clients ladder, the every season plan and job math, on a one-page offer sheet.
promises.quote: Home size, stories and service in; a quote, a text and an invoice out.
promises.keep: A thank-you, an honest review ask, next season's plan, a referral ask and a mid-season check-in, each dated, plus review cards with your QR code.
promises.sample_one: A free demo for one street or one partner business: door hangers or a sample letter, a card to send and every message, saved to your Pipeline.
promises.reply: Paste what someone wrote back: what they meant, a short answer with one next step, and your Pipeline updated. A draft you send yourself.
promises.won: Log the yes, then everything for the job: the booking text, a prep text, a printable job sheet, the after-job text and the invoice.
promises.proof: One lit house turned into proof: a result card, a before-and-after collage from your photos, a caption, an honest review ask and a case study once they say yes.
promises.next_25: The next 25 HOAs, agents, shops, churches and restaurants near you that are not in your Pipeline yet, with messages, saved for Do my day.
promises.ready: Look ready before you reach out: a one-page website, a Google profile kit and a flyer, all from your real prices.
promises.same_street: One customer's street turned into a route: door hangers with a neighbor price, a sheet for the 20 nearest homes and an intro ask for your customer.
promises.season_plan: Twelve months of offers: installs in the fall, takedowns in January, next season booked in the slow months, with a calendar file and a one-page plan.
promises.roofline_plan: Roofline, tree and walkway lengths in; feet of lights, clips, cords, circuits, material cost, a price per foot, a design sheet and the takedown dates out.

off_season.play: Book next season's installs now with a deposit, while installers have open calendars, and offer to hang and take down lights people already own.

crowd.note: Busy October to January: installs in the fall, takedowns in January. Slow February to August, when you book next season.
not_yet: Don't buy a lift or a truckload of lights before you have booked homes.
Don't add outlets, open a panel or splice into house wiring. That is an electrician's job.
Don't climb a second story before you have ladder practice, a helper and insurance.
crowd.basis: Scores, first $1, buyer and not-yet lines: our judgment, written up with their sources in research/niches/lights.json crowd_scores. Best months and slow season: Jobber, Brite Nites, Fixr and HomeAdvisor in research/niches/lights.json.

items.what_to_check: Plug lights into existing outdoor outlets only. A new outlet, a new circuit or any change to house wiring is a job for a licensed electrician: most light installers aren't certified for electrical work. Who may do electrical work differs by place, so check your city and state.

sources.says: Need new outdoor wiring? Budget $50 to $100 per hour for a licensed electrician; most light installers aren't certified for electrical work.
Some lighting installations may require modification to electrical wiring, which is a task that should always be done by a trained professional.

items.what_to_check: The National Electrical Code requires GFCI protection for outdoor receptacles at homes. Plug lights only into a GFCI-protected outlet or a portable GFCI, and use lights and cords rated for outdoor use. Your city and state adopt a code edition, so check your city and state.

sources.publisher: NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2025 edition, first draft working text)
sources.says: First Revision to 210.8(A), dwelling units: all 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles installed outdoors and supplied by single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground shall have ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel.

Check outdoor lights for labels showing they have been certified for outdoor use, and only plug them into a ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protected receptacle or a portable GFCI. Only use lights tested for safety by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.

items.what_to_check: Lights left on for 3 hours or more are a continuous load, and the code sizes the breaker at 125% of a continuous load. So keep the lights on one circuit to 80% of its breaker: 1,440 watts on a 15 amp circuit and 1,920 watts on a 20 amp circuit at 120 volts. Check which code edition your city and state use.

sources.publisher: NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2025 edition, first draft working text)
sources.says: 210.20(A): where a branch circuit supplies continuous loads, the rating of the overcurrent device shall not be less than the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load.

sources.publisher: NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2023 edition, second draft statements)
sources.says: Continuous load: a load where the maximum current is expected to continue for 3 hours or more.

items.what_to_check: Rails at least 3 feet above the roof edge if you step onto the roof, the base about a quarter of the ladder's working length out (1 foot for every 4 feet of ladder), stable and level footing, nonconductive rails near power, face the ladder and keep one hand on it, never stand on the top step of a stepladder, and carry nothing that could throw you off balance. OSHA rules bind employers and their workers; they are good practice for you, and they apply once you hire help. Edges 4 feet or more above a lower level need fall protection for workers.

sources.says: 1910.23(c)(11): side rails extend at least 3 feet above the upper landing surface; (c)(4): ladders used only on stable and level surfaces unless secured or stabilized; (c)(8): the cap and top step of a stepladder are not used as steps; (b)(11): face the ladder when climbing up or down; (b)(12): at least one hand grasps the ladder; (b)(13): no object or load that could cause a loss of balance; (b)(8): used only for the purposes they were designed.

1926.1053(b)(1): side rails at least 3 feet above the upper landing; (b)(5)(i): non-self-supporting ladders at an angle where the base is about one-quarter of the working length out; (b)(6): stable and level surfaces; (b)(12): nonconductive siderails near exposed energized equipment; (b)(13): never use the top step of a stepladder as a step; (b)(20): face the ladder; (b)(21): at least one hand on the ladder; (b)(22): never carry a load that could cause a loss of balance.

1910.28(b)(1)(i): the employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet or more above a lower level by guardrails, safety nets or personal fall protection.

items.what_to_check: Look up before you set the ladder: keep yourself, the ladder and the lights at least 10 feet from overhead power lines (lines of 50 kV or less). Call the utility if lines run near the roof.

sources.says: 1910.333(c)(3)(i)(A)(1): an unqualified person working in an elevated position near overhead lines, and the longest conductive object they may contact, stay at least 10 feet from unguarded, energized lines of 50 kV or less to ground.

steps: Before the install: a written plan (Roofline plan makes one) with the runs measured, the outlets and breakers you will use, the install and takedown dates and the price.
Test each outdoor outlet with a GFCI tester. Plug only into a GFCI-protected outlet or a portable GFCI.
Test every strand on the ground before it goes up. Throw out sets with cracked sockets or frayed or bare wire.
Look up first: keep yourself, the ladder and the lights 10 feet from power lines.

Set the ladder on stable, level ground with the base 1 foot out for every 4 feet of ladder, and the rails 3 feet above the roof edge if you step off. Face it, keep one hand on it, and have a helper steady it.
Hang with clips only, never nails, staples or tape: one clip per bulb on gutters and shingles.
Keep each circuit under 80% of its breaker and each cord under its label rating. Set the timer for the evening hours.
Walk the house at dusk, fix any dark bulb, take the photo from the street and put the takedown date in writing.

sources.says: 1910.23: side rails at least 3 feet above the upper landing, stable and level surfaces, face the ladder, at least one hand on it, no load that could cause a loss of balance.
1926.1053(b)(5)(i): the base of a non-self-supporting ladder about one-quarter of the working length out from the support.
Unqualified persons in an elevated position stay 10 feet from energized overhead lines of 50 kV or less.

Check outdoor lights for labels showing they have been certified for outdoor use, and only plug them into a ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protected receptacle or a portable GFCI. Only use lights tested for safety by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.

Check each set of lights, new or old, for broken or cracked sockets, frayed or bare wires, or loose connections; throw out damaged sets. Check each extension cord to make sure it is rated for the intended use and is in good condition.

sources.says: 210.20(A): where a branch circuit supplies continuous loads, the rating of the overcurrent device shall not be less than the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load.
Refrain from using tape to hang Christmas lights: if they get hot, the tape can ignite. Professionals use a ladder, light clips, extension cords and wiring.
Test outdoor outlets and, if you're unsure, bring in an electrician; never work alone, a helper steadies the ladder.
Leave Christmas lights on for no more than 4 to 6 hours in the evening.

job_checklist.note: The order, the written plan and the dusk walk are common practice, a judgment call. OSHA rules bind employers; they are good practice for you too.

same_street.headline: Your neighbor price on {street}

includes: Commercial LED lights supplied for the season
Clipped and hung straight, no nails or tape

how: Text me your address or scan the code
same_street.customer_ask: Hi {customer}, thanks again! I'm lighting a couple more homes on {street}{day_part}. If a neighbor asks who hung your lights, would you pass on my number{phone_part}? It means a lot to a new business.
steps: Hang a door hanger on every home on this sheet the day before you install there. On the door, never in or on a mailbox.
While you install, say hi to anyone outside. Keep it short, and never say which neighbor: "I'm lighting a home here on your street."
Text your customer the intro ask after the install, never before.
Mark each home on the sheet. A neighbor who books goes on the same install day as your customer.
same_street.why: Homes on one street mean less driving and loading between installs and takedowns, so you can give neighbors a better price on the same day.

who.takedown: Every customer you lit this season, then their neighbors
who.book_early: Last season's customers first, then everyone who asked too late
who.early_install: Last season's customers, then neighbors, HOAs and real estate agents
who.main: People you know, neighbors of each customer, shops and restaurants

do.takedown: Take down and box every display from January 2, and ask each customer to book next season while you are there.
do.book_early: Book next season's installs now with a small deposit, earliest install dates first.
do.early_install: Offer early install dates before the Thanksgiving rush, one street at a time.
do.main: Fill each install day on one or two streets before you add a new area.

plans: Every season plan: the same lights hung each fall and taken down each January, booked again at the takedown.
Install and takedown for people who own their lights: the same visits, their lights.
A free roofline measure with a printed plan: the sample that gets you onto a street.
